volumes.title: The Bell That Wasn't There
volumes.text:
On the Tuesday before Founders' Day, Emberwick woke late. Nobody could say why until Mrs. Applin the baker looked up from her doorstep and saw daylight through the top of the market cross, where for two hundred years there had been a bell. Old Tabitha, three hundredweight of bronze, was gone.

Inspector Hubert Marrow arrived at eight with a notebook, a paper of peppermints and Constable Daisy Pim, who was new and keen. He had heard every joke there was about his surname and vegetables, and he waited patiently while the crowd made them again.

"Nine days to Founders' Day," said the Mayor. "She must ring it in, Inspector. She always has." Marrow looked up at the empty beam. The bell rope lay at the foot of the cross, coiled as neatly as a sleeping cat. He wrote that down first.

volumes.title: A Neatly Coiled Rope
volumes.text:
Inspector Marrow climbed the ladder inside Emberwick's market cross himself, which Constable Pim thought brave for a man of his width. The market bell, Old Tabitha, had been stolen in the night, and he wished to see how.

The four bolts that had held her to the beam lay in a row on the ledge. They had been unscrewed, not sawn, and somebody had oiled the threads first. The little door at the foot of the cross had been opened with a key and locked again afterwards. Below, the bell rope was coiled and tied off with a tidy hitch.

"Thieves cut ropes," Marrow said, coming down rather faster than he went up. "They break locks. They do not tidy." He offered Pim a peppermint. "Whoever took her, Constable, was fond of her. Find out who holds a key to that door."

volumes.title: The Baker's Ear
volumes.text:
Mrs. Applin the baker rose at four every morning and missed very little. Inspector Marrow, looking into the theft of Emberwick's market bell, called on her while the loaves were still warm, and was given one for his trouble. She had heard no hammering on the night Old Tabitha vanished, and no horse. "A squeak, perhaps, around midnight. I took it for a gate."

"But I'll tell you what I did hear," she said, thumping dough. "All last week that bell rang wrong. Ever since the hard frost. She used to ring round, like a plum. Last week she rang flat, like a dropped pan. I said so to Mr. Fenn the crier, and he told me my ears wanted syringing."

Marrow wrote down flat, and frost, and squeak, and underlined none of them yet. Then he asked what she charged for a second loaf.

volumes.title: Mr. Lobb's Cart
volumes.text:
When three hundredweight of bronze goes missing, a town looks first at its scrap dealer. Mr. Lobb of Tanner's Row knew this, and met Inspector Marrow at his gate with his arms already folded. "I buy kettles," he said. "I don't buy bells. Who would I sell Old Tabitha to? Everyone from here to the Grey Coast knows her voice."

Marrow admired the logic and looked at the cart anyway. Its wheels ran true. In the mud beside Emberwick's market cross, Constable Pim had found a single narrow track that wandered from side to side, the mark of a wheel that wobbled. Mr. Lobb's did not. He had also spent the night at his sister's in Sallowby, where eleven people had watched him lose at dominoes.

"Then I apologise for the visit," said Marrow. Mr. Lobb unfolded his arms and offered tea.

volumes.title: The Sallowby Theory
volumes.text:
Half of Emberwick was certain that Sallowby had taken the market bell. Sallowby had envied Old Tabitha for two centuries, the argument ran, and envy is patient. So Inspector Marrow and Constable Pim walked the four miles over on a damp Thursday to ask.

Sallowby was offended, and then delighted to be offended. The churchwarden showed them the village's own bell, new last spring, and rang it for them twice. "What would we want with yours? Ours is in tune."

On the way home Pim stopped at the crossroads. In the soft verge ran the same wandering wheel track they had found by the market cross. It did not go toward Sallowby at all. It turned north and ended at the first milestone, where a wagon and two horses had stood waiting. Up that road there was nothing for nine miles but sheep, weather and the foundry at Cinderhowe.

volumes.title: Three Keys
volumes.text:
Three keys opened the little door of Emberwick's market cross, and Inspector Marrow, hunting the thief of the market bell, went to see all three.

The Mayor's hung on a nail in the Guildhall, so rusted to the nail that it took pliers to lift. Miss Dobbs, who wound the town clock, had dropped hers in the river Ember in April and could name four witnesses. The third belonged to Mr. Osric Fenn, town crier and ringer of the bell for thirty-one years. It shone on his belt.

Mr. Fenn was grieved and loud. He demanded arrests. He offered five pounds of his own savings as a reward, and blew his nose on a red spotted handkerchief. Walking back, Constable Pim remarked that in all that noise he had never once asked where the bell might be. Marrow had noticed too.

volumes.title: Turnips and Lozenges
volumes.text:
Three boys from Ember Lane came to the police house on Friday with their caps off, pushed from behind by a mother. They had something to confess to Inspector Marrow about the night Emberwick's market bell was stolen.

They had meant to hang a turnip in Old Tabitha's place, for a joke. But when they crept into the square at midnight the bell was already down, and a handcart was going away up Guildhall Street with a hooded lantern. One wheel squeaked. The person pushing it stopped at the horse trough and wet the axle, and after that it went quietly.

"We found this where the cart stood," said the smallest, and put a sticky brown lozenge on the desk. Horehound, for sore throats. Marrow, a peppermint man, studied it with respect. He confiscated the turnip, which made a good soup.

volumes.title: The Wobbling Wheel
volumes.text:
Constable Daisy Pim found the cart on Saturday. It had taken her two days and most of Emberwick's back yards, and Inspector Marrow, who was investigating the theft of the market bell, said afterwards that it was the best piece of work in the case.

It stood in the yard behind the Guildhall, a flat handcart used for moving chairs on concert nights. The left wheel leaned on its axle and wobbled when she pushed it. The spokes were caked with red clay, and there is no red clay in Emberwick. It lies up on the Fells road. In the cart bed were two fresh grooves, the width of a bell's lip.

The shed where the cart lived was kept locked. The caretaker said only four people ever borrowed the key: the Mayor, the clerk, himself, and Mr. Fenn the crier.

volumes.title: The Foundry at Cinderhowe
volumes.text:
Inspector Marrow hired a pony and rode up the Fells road to Cinderhowe alone, following a hunch about Emberwick's missing market bell. The foundry sat in a fold of the hills, smoking gently, like a kettle someone had forgotten.

Mrs. Brask the founder was a broad woman in a leather apron. She would not show him the casting floor. "I don't discuss customers' orders," she said. Customers, Marrow noted, not thieves. Through the door behind her he could see a pit, and in the pit a tall clay mould the shape of a bell.

He asked instead, as a matter of general interest, what happened to a bell rung in a hard frost. "Cracks, like as not," said Mrs. Brask. "Then she rings flat as a pan. Can't be mended. Has to be melted and cast again." He rode home slowly, thinking about a baker's ears.

volumes.title: Frost in the Ringing Book
volumes.text:
The ringing book of Emberwick's market cross lives in a drawer at the Guildhall, and the first rule is pasted inside its cover: the bell shall not be rung in hard frost, but a handbell used instead. Inspector Marrow, five days into the affair of the stolen bell, read it on Sunday afternoon with his boots off.

The morning of the great frost, a fortnight back, had its entry like every other day. Rang seven, as usual, O. Fenn. But "as usual" had been scratched through afterwards in a blacker ink, and the handbell in the drawer wore a year of dust.

On Monday he met the crier in the square. Mr. Fenn's voice was hoarse and his thumb was bandaged, and along both shirt cuffs ran a faint green stain, the green that old bronze leaves on anything that hugs it. "Any news, Inspector?" "Some," said Marrow.

volumes.title: Marrow Polishes His Boots
volumes.text:
Inspector Marrow did his best thinking with a tin of blacking and a brush. On the Tuesday night, a week after the market bell vanished from Emberwick, Constable Pim found him at the police house table with both boots off.

"Consider our thief," he said, working at a toecap. "He oils the bolts. He coils the rope. He wets a squeaking axle so as not to wake the baker. He drops a throat lozenge. He takes the bell not to a scrap yard but toward a foundry, a week after she began to ring flat." He held the boot to the light. "That is not a thief, Pim. That is a man with a bad conscience and a very sore throat."

Pim said a name. Marrow nodded, and asked her to invite the Mayor, the baker and the crier to the market cross at dusk tomorrow.

volumes.title: Old Tabitha Comes Home
volumes.text:
At dusk on the eve of Founders' Day a wagon came down the Fells road into Emberwick with something large under a tarpaulin. Inspector Marrow was waiting at the market cross with the Mayor, the baker and Mr. Fenn the town crier, who had gone the colour of candle wax.

"I rang her in the frost," Mr. Fenn said. "Thirty-one years, and I forgot the rule once. She cracked. I couldn't stand in this square and say so." He had spent his savings on having her cast again at Cinderhowe, meaning to hang her back unnoticed.

Marrow charged him with borrowing the Guildhall handcart without leave. The Mayor fined him a shilling and the price of a new wheel. They hung the bell by lantern light, and in the morning she rang round as a plum. Mrs. Applin, at her oven, said that was more like it.

volumes.title: Cocoa Gone Cold
volumes.text:
The morning after the Harvest Supper, Mrs. Gantry carried a duster into the vicarage study at Thrushcombe and came out again without it. Mr. Ambrose Thackle, churchwarden and parish treasurer, was sitting in the vicar's armchair with a cup of cocoa gone cold at his elbow. He had been there all night, and he would not be getting up.

Miss Clementine Aske, the vicar's sister, kept the house, the accounts and eleven hives of bees, and was not easily flustered. She shut the study door, sent the garden boy for Dr. Peabody and Sergeant Dunnock, and sat her brother down with tea before telling him.

"Poor Thackle," said the Reverend Barnaby Aske. "Nobody liked him, you know. I always meant to." Clementine was thinking about the cup. Under the smell of chocolate there had been another smell, one she knew from the hedgerows and could not yet place.

volumes.title: What the Doctor Found
volumes.text:
Dr. Peabody was a cautious man who disliked saying anything before lunch. But by noon on the day Mr. Thackle was found in the vicarage study at Thrushcombe, he had said it twice. The churchwarden's cocoa had contained widow's thimble, a purple hedge flower that no cook could mistake for anything else.

"Then somebody put it there," said Sergeant Dunnock, and wrote murder in his notebook, slowly, as if the word might bite. Twenty-three people had sat down to the Harvest Supper. He began a list.

Miss Clementine Aske, the vicar's sister, was already ahead of him. Every guest had drunk cocoa from the same pan and gone home well. Only the study cup was wrong. It had been poured at nine and left on a tray on the hall table, because Mr. Thackle liked to do the supper accounts alone. For ten minutes that tray had stood unwatched.

volumes.title: A Hymn Sung Flat
volumes.text:
Miss Clementine Aske asked everyone at Thrushcombe vicarage the same question: where were you during the last hymn? It was then, at nine on the night of the Harvest Supper, that a cup of cocoa had stood alone in the hall, and by morning it had done for Mr. Thackle.

Nearly everybody had been in the parlour, singing. They remembered it, because it had been dreadful. Mr. Vane the organist, who should have been at the piano, had mislaid his spectacles again and gone to hunt for them, so the hymn went up without him and came down in several places at once.

Three people, then, were out of the room. Mr. Vane, peering under cushions. Mrs. Gantry, in the kitchen with the pans. And Farmer Rudge, who had put on his hat at ten to nine and left without a goodnight.

volumes.title: Farmer Rudge's Temper
volumes.text:
Sergeant Dunnock liked Farmer Rudge for the murder at Thrushcombe vicarage. Jed Rudge owed the dead churchwarden two quarters' rent. At the Harvest Supper he had said, before the whole table, that Mr. Thackle would squeeze a turnip and charge it for the juice. Then he had left early, at the very hour the cocoa stood unguarded in the hall.

Miss Clementine Aske, the vicar's sister, walked up to the farm to hear his side. Rudge was in the byre, red in the face and gentle in the hands, with a calf two days old.

"She came on the night of the supper," he said. "My boy ran down for me at ten to nine. Ask him. Ask the cow." The calf was called Harvest. Clementine scratched its ears, believed him, and went home to tell the sergeant, who was sorry to lose so tidy a suspect.

volumes.title: A Hat on the Pond
volumes.text:
Two days after Mr. Thackle was found in the study, Thrushcombe had a second shock. Mr. Leopold Vane, the organist, did not come to play for the evening service. The vicar gave out the psalm unaccompanied, and afterwards the garden boy found a grey felt hat floating on the vicarage pond, with L.V. inked inside the band.

By supper the village was saying murders, in the plural, and rather enjoying the extra letter. Sergeant Dunnock had the pond dragged. This did not take long, since it is two feet deep in the middle. It gave up a boot, a croquet ball and a large indignant carp.

"No organist," said Miss Clementine Aske, the vicar's sister, watching from the bank. "Carried off, then," said the sergeant. "Perhaps," said Clementine. She was looking at the hat. It had been found the right way up, and the crown was perfectly dry.

volumes.title: The Second-Best Hat
volumes.text:
Mrs. Tibbs let rooms above the saddler's in Thrushcombe, and for nine years the best of them had been Mr. Vane's. Now the organist was missing, his hat had been fished from the vicarage pond, and the village counted him a second victim. Miss Clementine Aske, the vicar's sister, asked to see the room.

"That hat they found was his second-best," said Mrs. Tibbs, opening the wardrobe. "His best is gone. So are his good boots, his travelling bag and that ticking thing off the piano. His metronome. And he paid me to the end of the month on Saturday, in new coins, him that was always three weeks behind."

She sniffed. "He'd turned peculiar besides. Wore his gloves indoors ever since the supper, even at breakfast. Said September had got into his fingers." Clementine thanked her. A man does not generally pack for his own murder.

volumes.title: Where Widow's Thimble Grows
volumes.text:
Miss Clementine Aske knew every plant in Thrushcombe, since her bees visited most of them. Widow's thimble, the purple flower that had found its way into Mr. Thackle's cocoa at the vicarage, is fussy. It will not grow in a garden. In the whole parish it grows in one place: along the north wall of the churchyard, beside the small door to the organ loft.

She went to look. A patch as wide as a tea tray had been cut, cleanly, with scissors. Whoever did it had stood on the organ-loft step to reach.

There is one more thing to know about widow's thimble. Its juice shows nothing at first. By the next morning it comes up violet on the skin, and no soap will shift it for a week. Clementine stood a while, considering who in the village had lately kept his hands covered.

volumes.title: Mrs. Gantry's Candles
volumes.text:
Sergeant Dunnock, having lost Farmer Rudge, turned his notebook toward Mrs. Gantry. She had made the cocoa on the night Mr. Thackle died at Thrushcombe vicarage. She had also quarrelled with him that very week, when the churchwarden docked fourpence from the housekeeping for what he called an extravagance of candles.

"Fourpence," said Mrs. Gantry, with her arms in the sink. "If I poisoned every man who was mean about candles, Sergeant, there'd be no vestry meetings."

Miss Clementine Aske, the vicar's sister, settled it more quietly. Twenty-two people drank from Mrs. Gantry's pan and took no harm, so the pan was innocent, and so was the kitchen. The mischief was done in the hall, to one cup, during the last hymn. And all through that hymn Mrs. Gantry had been heard through the wall, banging pans in a temper. Even the sergeant agreed nobody bangs pans from the hall.

volumes.title: The Treasurer's Notebook
volumes.text:
Mr. Ambrose Thackle had not been loved in Thrushcombe, but he had been exact. In his waistcoat, on the morning he was found in the vicarage study, was a notebook ruled in red, and Sergeant Dunnock let Miss Clementine Aske read it at the kitchen table.

It held pew rents, coal, the Harvest Supper down to the last halfpenny bun. The final entry was different. "Organ Fund. Six years of jumble sales and no pipes. Shall count the box on Friday. Have told L.V. so, as is only fair."

The Reverend Barnaby Aske, called in from the garden, remembered something. At the supper Thackle had asked him for the key to the vestry chest, where the Organ Fund box was kept. "He asked me across the table," said the vicar. "Quite loudly. Mr. Vane was passing the pickles, and dropped the spoon."

volumes.title: Buttons in the Box
volumes.text:
The Organ Fund box at Thrushcombe had sat in the vestry chest for six years, growing heavier after every jumble sale. Mr. Thackle, the treasurer, had meant to count it, and had died in the vicarage study the night before he could. So Miss Clementine Aske, the vicar's sister, counted it for him, with Sergeant Dunnock holding the lamp.

The box was heavy. It rattled handsomely. It contained two hundred and six trouser buttons, iron washers and a flat grey stone. "Somebody," said the sergeant, "has been at this."

Only two people ever handled the box, Clementine told him: the treasurer who locked it away, and the organist who carried it round at concerts. And the organ still wheezed on its lowest note. She had written to the pipe makers in Emberwick, and their answer lay on the table. No order from Thrushcombe had ever been placed.

volumes.title: The Carrier's Passenger
volumes.text:
Old Mr. Hobb the carrier drives from Thrushcombe to the coast every Monday and talks to nobody but his horse. Miss Clementine Aske, the vicar's sister, brought him a jar of honey and asked whether he had carried anyone on the Monday after the organist disappeared.

He had. A gentleman had waved him down at the crossroads a mile beyond the village, before light, wrapped to the nose in a muffler. Gloves on. He had ridden all the way to Saltmouth harbour without a word. "Only his bag talked," said Mr. Hobb. "Went tick, tock, tick, every time we hit a rut. Like a clock that couldn't make up its mind."

Clementine thought of a metronome missing from a piano, and a hat with a dry crown. She walked straight to Sergeant Dunnock, who heard her out and sent for the fastest horse in the parish.

volumes.title: Only the One Murder
volumes.text:
They found Mr. Leopold Vane at the Ship Inn in Saltmouth, calling himself a traveller in ribbons. He might have passed, but there was a piano and he had not been able to leave it alone. Nobody in ribbons plays like that.

Miss Clementine Aske set it out for Sergeant Dunnock. For six years the organist of Thrushcombe had emptied the Organ Fund and filled the box with buttons. Warned that Mr. Thackle meant to count it, he cut widow's thimble by the loft door, slipped out of the Harvest Supper during the last hymn, and saw to the cup on the hall table. Then he left a hat on the vicarage pond, to be mourned instead of hunted. His fingers, when the gloves came off, were violet.

Thrushcombe gave up its plural with regret. The fund began again, and the vicar's sister kept the box.

volumes.title: The Board Said Seven-Forty
volumes.text:
Every morning at six Miss Maud Tern chalks the tides on the board outside the Post and Tide Office at Cocklesand, on the Grey Coast. Low water, and the hours when the causeway to Gull Rock is safe. People walk out by that board. She has kept it nineteen years without a slip.

On a Wednesday in October the cocklers went down at dawn and found Mr. Jasper Crale on the sands below the causeway. He was a visitor, a salvage man from inland, who walked out to the old wreck by Gull Rock every evening. The tide had come round behind him in the dusk, and he had not got back.

Captain Rudd the harbourmaster read the board with his jaw set. Low water, 7.40. The true time had been 6.40. "An hour out, Maud," he said. "And a man is dead of it."

volumes.title: A Seven With a Bar
volumes.text:
Miss Maud Tern of the Tide Office at Cocklesand did not sleep the night after Mr. Crale was found on the sands. Her board had sent him out to Gull Rock an hour late, the harbourmaster said, and the sea had done the rest.

At first light she opened her daybook, where each morning she copies what she has chalked. Tuesday: low water 6.40, in her own square hand. Then she went outside with a lamp and looked at the board.

The 7 of 7.40 had a little bar through its stem. Miss Tern has never barred a seven in her life. Her mother thought it foreign and her schoolmistress thought it showy. Under the figure, when she tilted the lamp, the ghost of a rubbed-out 6 still showed. She had made no slip. Somebody had changed one figure, and left the rest to the tide.

volumes.title: Two Kinds of Chalk
volumes.text:
Constable Ned Lugg of Cocklesand is a slow, fair man who mends nets when he is thinking. Miss Maud Tern brought him to the tide board, the board that had sent Mr. Crale out to Gull Rock an hour too late, and made him put his nose to it.

"My chalk comes off the cliff," she said. "I cut it myself. It's soft and greyish and it crumbles." She drew a line to show him. "Now look at that seven." The false figure was a hard, bright white. Lugg knew it at once. It was the stick chalk kept in a saucer by the skittle board at the Anchor Inn, where half the village scored its Saturday nights.

"That narrows it to everybody," he said. "Everybody who was in the Anchor," said Miss Tern, "and passed my board before dusk on Tuesday. It's a start, Ned."

volumes.title: Wet Tar at Four
volumes.text:
Tom Skerry tarred the post of the tide board at Cocklesand at four o'clock on the Tuesday. By nightfall Mr. Crale had walked out to Gull Rock by a false figure on that board and been caught by the sea. Constable Lugg thought the two facts sat close together.

Tom had reason to dislike the man. His grandfather had been mate of the Marigold, wrecked off Gull Rock sixty years ago, and Crale had bought the salvage rights from under the village for eleven pounds. Tom had said things in the Anchor. He was also tarred to the elbows.

Miss Maud Tern of the Tide Office looked at the post instead. At elbow height was a smear in the tar, where somebody had leaned in to reach the board. "After four, then, while it was wet," she said. "And Tom would never have smudged his own work."

volumes.title: A Clerk With Dry Feet
volumes.text:
Mr. Jasper Crale, lost to the tide at Gull Rock, had left one mourner in Cocklesand. Mr. Edwin Larch had been his clerk for fifteen years. He was a pale, tidy man who folded his napkin, and he sat in the parlour of the Anchor Inn like someone waiting for a train.

Miss Maud Tern of the Tide Office, whose board had been tampered with on the evening Crale died, brought the inn's post herself to meet him. She asked whether he had ever walked out to the wreck with his employer.

"Never once," said Mr. Larch. "I cannot abide wet feet. Mr. Crale went alone, every evening. On Tuesday I was in my room from tea until ten, writing his letters." Mrs. Pennant the landlady remarked that Mr. Crale had owed her three weeks' board, and she supposed the sea would not be paying it.

volumes.title: No Letters in the Bag
volumes.text:
In Cocklesand the postmistress and the tide keeper are the same woman, which is how Miss Maud Tern came to know something the constable did not. Mr. Larch, clerk to the drowned Mr. Crale, said he had spent Tuesday evening at the Anchor Inn writing letters. But every letter leaving the village passes through her hands, and since Tuesday the Anchor had posted nothing except the cook's order for seeds.

She asked Mrs. Pennant about that evening. A supper tray had gone up to Mr. Larch's door at half past five. At eight it was still on the mat.

"Perhaps he writes slowly," said Constable Lugg. "Perhaps he wasn't there," said Miss Tern. Somebody had altered her tide board that afternoon, and a man had died at Gull Rock because of it. She wrote Larch on a slip and put it in the drawer with the stamps.

volumes.title: The Captain's Sevens
volumes.text:
Miss Maud Tern is a fair woman, so she suspected her own harbourmaster too. Captain Rudd had quarrelled with Mr. Crale over harbour dues. He initials the tide board at Cocklesand every week, and knew what an hour's error would do on the Gull Rock causeway. And when Crale was found on the sands, he had been very quick to say the mistake was hers.

The false figure on her board was a seven with a bar through it. So she asked to see the harbour dues book and read six months of the captain's sums. His sevens were as plain as fence posts.

Besides, from five until nine on the Tuesday he had been chairing the lifeboat committee at the chapel hall, before eleven people and a plate of rock cakes. Miss Tern closed the book. She was relieved, and a little ashamed, and mentioned neither.

volumes.title: What Crale Wrote Down
volumes.text:
They had found a pocket diary on Mr. Jasper Crale, the salvage man caught by the tide at Gull Rock, and Constable Lugg of Cocklesand had dried it on the rack above his stove. On Friday he showed it to Miss Maud Tern, since she read handwriting for a living.

Most of it was sums. Crale had spent a month poking about the bones of the Marigold, which lie in the sand by the rock and show only at low water. The last entry was made on the Monday, the day before he died. "Under the third rib from the stern. A box, iron-bound. Cannot shift it alone. Tell nobody but L. Bring crowbar when the tide serves."

"L," said the constable. "That's me, Lugg. Only he never told me a thing." "No, Ned," said Miss Tern gently. "I don't think he meant you."

volumes.title: Red Weed and a Receipt
volumes.text:
Pip, the boot boy at the Anchor Inn in Cocklesand, is eleven and notices everything below the knee. He told Miss Maud Tern that Mr. Larch's boots, put out on Thursday morning, had been wet through, with red ribbon weed stuck in the welts. That weed grows on Gull Rock and nowhere else on the coast. Yet Mr. Larch, clerk to the drowned Mr. Crale, swore he had never been out there.

His grey coat had gone to Mrs. Oake the laundress with a black smear on the left elbow that no soap would move. Tar, she said, and him a gentleman.

Then Mrs. Pennant showed Miss Tern the receipt Mr. Larch had written when he settled the bill. 17s. 7d., in a clerk's neat hand. Each seven had a little bar through its stem. Miss Tern put on her hat and went to find the constable.

volumes.title: Springs on Saturday
volumes.text:
"It's a smear, some seaweed and a way of writing sevens," said Constable Lugg. "A magistrate would laugh at me, Maud." He was right, and Miss Tern of the Cocklesand Tide Office knew it. They believed Mr. Larch the clerk had altered her board to drown his employer at Gull Rock. They could not prove it.

So she took down her tables. The iron-bound box Mr. Crale had found lay under the wreck of the Marigold. The lowest tide of the month, the spring tide, fell on Saturday evening at a quarter past eight. Only then would the third rib stand clear long enough for one man with a crowbar.

On Saturday morning she chalked the board, true to the minute, where anyone staying at the Anchor might read it. Then she asked Tom Skerry to have his boat ready at seven.

volumes.title: Waiting on Gull Rock
volumes.text:
At seven on Saturday evening Tom Skerry rowed Miss Maud Tern and Constable Lugg round to the seaward side of Gull Rock, a mile off Cocklesand, and they sat down among the red weed to wait. It was cold. The constable had brought a net to mend and could not see to mend it.

The tide went out and out, further than it goes all month. The causeway lay bare and shining. Near the rock the old ribs of the Marigold came up through the sand one by one, black and crooked, like a comb with teeth missing. Somewhere among them Mr. Crale had found a box, and had not lived to lift it.

A little after eight a lantern left the shore. It came steadily along the causeway, held low. Whoever carried it knew the hour exactly, and had something long and heavy over one shoulder.

volumes.title: The Tide Keeps Time
volumes.text:
It was Mr. Edwin Larch who knelt at the third rib of the Marigold with a crowbar, and Constable Lugg who stood up out of the weed on Gull Rock and wished him good evening. He did not run. There is nowhere to run on a causeway.

He told it on the walk back to Cocklesand. Fifteen years a clerk, and when Mr. Crale found the box he had promised him nothing from it. So Larch took chalk from the Anchor and turned a six into a seven. "I only changed one figure," he said. "It was the figure people walk out by," said Miss Maud Tern.

The box, opened at the Tide Office, held forty pewter buttons and a ship's spoon. Captain Rudd apologised, before witnesses. On Sunday at six Miss Tern chalked the tides, low water and safe hours, her sevens as plain as ever.

volumes.title: The Problem Stated
volumes.text:
The Locked Room Quarterly exists to examine impossible things calmly. We have forty-one subscribers and, this season, one problem worth all of them.

At Thistledown House, on the edge of Emberwick, Mr. Lucian Thrupp keeps sixty-one clocks in a room at the top of the stairs. Each Sunday before two he bolts himself in and dozes until four. Last Sunday, he tells us, the Winter Queen, a gold travelling clock no bigger than a plum, was wound and put to bed in her leather case on his table before he shot the bolt. At three he heard her chime, three silver notes going down. At four he opened the case and it was empty.

The door was bolted on the inside. The window has been painted shut for twenty years. The chimney would not admit a cat. Mr. Thrupp was alone. We invite theories, by post.

volumes.title: The Secret Passage Theory
volumes.text:
Nine subscribers have written to The Locked Room Quarterly proposing a sliding panel. We understand the appeal. The Clock Room at Thistledown House was bolted from within, its owner asleep in his chair, and a gold clock the size of a plum left it all the same.

We therefore spent a Tuesday with Mr. Tull the builder, tapping. The walls are stone, two feet thick, behind honest plaster. The ceiling is sound. Under the one loose floorboard we found a button, a dead moth and a penny older than Mr. Tull. No panel. No passage.

We did learn the room's habits. All sixty-one clocks are kept by Mr. Enoch Vesper of Emberwick, who has come at one every Sunday for nineteen years to wind them. He winds the little Winter Queen last, settles her in her case, and is gone before Mr. Thrupp bolts the door.

volumes.title: The Thread and Bolt Theory
volumes.text:
A retired locksmith in Sallowby writes that any bolt may be shot from outside with a bent pin and a length of thread, and that the vanishing of the Winter Queen from Mr. Thrupp's Clock Room is no puzzle at all. The Locked Room Quarterly took him at his word and tried it.

We tried it for a wet afternoon. The door at Thistledown House fits its frame like a cork in a bottle. No thread passes under it, and the keyhole is blocked on the inside by a brass plate. The bolt itself is as thick as a thumb, and so stiff that Mr. Thrupp uses both hands. We broke four pins and the editor's temper.

A key, several readers suggest. But a key does nothing against a bolt. Mr. Thrupp shot it himself, at five to two, directly after seeing his clock winder to the stair.

volumes.title: The Gardener at the Window
volumes.text:
Several subscribers ask about the window. A gold clock has vanished from the bolted Clock Room at Thistledown House, and a window is a kind of door. The Locked Room Quarterly climbed a ladder to see.

The window is painted shut. The paint is twenty years old and unbroken all round. The ladder belongs to Dob, the gardener, who spent that Sunday from two until half past three upon it, clipping the wisteria, with his face a foot from the glass.

Dob is a truthful man with no imagination, which makes him the perfect witness. He saw Mr. Thrupp asleep in his chair. He saw the little leather case on the table, shut. Nobody came in. Nothing moved but the pendulums. At three he heard a faint chime through the glass. We wrote down exactly what he saw, the case and not the clock, because exactness is our trade.

volumes.title: The Niece and the Jam
volumes.text:
A subscriber who signs herself Suspicious of Cinderhowe asks who gains. The Winter Queen, the little gold clock that vanished from the bolted Clock Room at Thistledown House, is worth more than the roof, and Mr. Thrupp's niece has long wished to open a bookshop.

Miss Sibyl Thrupp received The Locked Room Quarterly with sticky hands. On the Sunday in question she and Mrs. Marl the housekeeper made damson jam from half past one until five. Each swears to the other, and forty-three pots swear to both.

"I heard her chime at three, from the kitchen stair," Miss Sibyl told us. "I'd know her anywhere. Three notes going down, like somebody small coming downstairs." So the Winter Queen was heard at three by her owner, his niece and the gardener. We print this in good faith. We also note that an ear is not an eye.

volumes.title: The Owner Did It
volumes.text:
A gentleman in the Lowlands suggests that Mr. Lucian Thrupp, alone in his bolted Clock Room at Thistledown House, simply pocketed his own gold clock and cried thief. The Locked Room Quarterly has considered this with the seriousness it deserves.

The Winter Queen was never insured. Mr. Thrupp gains nothing by losing her, and has offered twenty pounds for her return. He sits among his sixty remaining clocks like a man at a party where the one guest he wanted has not come.

He also let us search. We spent a day in that room on our knees. We looked in the coal scuttle, the cushions and the case of every clock, though to an editor all clockwork looks alike. We found no gold clock the size of a plum. She left the room. We are sure of that much, and of nothing else.

volumes.title: The Chime Heard Again
volumes.text:
The Locked Room Quarterly does not hold with ghosts. We record, however, that on the Monday after the Winter Queen vanished from the Clock Room at Thistledown House, Mrs. Marl the housekeeper was dusting there at three o'clock and heard her chime. Three silver notes, going down. Mrs. Marl left the duster where it fell.

The little gold clock was not in the room. We had searched it. Emberwick decided by teatime that the house was haunted by a timepiece.

Your editor went up on Tuesday and sat in Mr. Thrupp's chair with the door open and a sandwich. At three, sixty clocks struck in their sixty voices, and under them, quite clearly, came three small notes descending. They did not come from the table. They came from the corner by the door, where the tall clock called Old Parliament stands. We finished the sandwich thoughtfully.

volumes.title: Mr. Vesper's Sunday
volumes.text:
The Locked Room Quarterly must examine the one outsider who entered the Clock Room at Thistledown House on the day the Winter Queen vanished. Mr. Enoch Vesper, clock mender of Emberwick, has wound Mr. Thrupp's sixty-one clocks every Sunday for nineteen years.

He arrived at one. He wound the tall clocks first and the little gold Winter Queen last, and closed her leather case on the table, with Mr. Thrupp looking on from the armchair. At five to two he was shown to the stair, and the bolt went home behind him.

From half past two until four he played the cornet with the Town Band on the bandstand, before two hundred people, several of whom wished he would play more quietly. The Winter Queen chimed in the bolted room at three. If that is so, Mr. Vesper is the one man in Emberwick who cannot have taken her.

volumes.title: The Maker's Mark
volumes.text:
A subscriber asks The Locked Room Quarterly where the Winter Queen came from, before she vanished from Mr. Thrupp's bolted Clock Room at Thistledown House. We ought to have asked sooner.

She was made in Emberwick sixty years ago. Under her dial, Mr. Thrupp tells us, are the letters E.V. and a small engraved snowflake. Her maker was Elias Vesper, who sold her one hard winter to pay for coal and regretted it until he died. Mr. Thrupp bought her at auction, quite fairly, forty years on.

Elias Vesper's grandson is Enoch, who winds the clocks at Thistledown. Every New Year's Day for nineteen years he has asked, hat in hand, to buy his grandfather's clock back at any price he could save. Every year Mr. Thrupp has said no. He mentioned it to us as an amusing habit of the man's. We did not find it amusing.

volumes.title: Inside Old Parliament
volumes.text:
For this number The Locked Room Quarterly brought in an expert. Mrs. Hester Lune mends clocks at Cinderhowe, owes nothing to anybody in Emberwick, and agreed to open the tall clock called Old Parliament, which stands by the door of the Clock Room at Thistledown House. It was from that corner that a chime was heard after the gold Winter Queen had gone.

She worked for ten minutes with a small screwdriver and then said, "Well, well."

Tucked behind the great brass wheels was a thing that had no business there: a steel comb with three teeth, a tiny hammer, and a pin set in the hour wheel to trip it at three o'clock exactly. Three notes, going down. The brass was bright. Mrs. Lune judged it less than a year old, and beautifully made. "Somebody," she said, "has taught this old fellow to do an impression."

volumes.title: A Challenge to Subscribers
volumes.text:
The Locked Room Quarterly now holds every fact in the matter of the Winter Queen, the gold clock that left a bolted room at Thistledown House while her owner slept. Before we print the answer we lay the facts out, and invite subscribers to send theirs first.

One. Nobody saw the clock itself after five to two. Mr. Thrupp, the gardener and our own search saw only a shut leather case. Two. The chime heard at three did not come from the Winter Queen. It came from a new device hidden in the tall clock. Three. So the chime proves nothing about where she was at three, and an alibi that rests upon it rests on air. Four. She was made by a Vesper.

Consider who closed the case, who winds the tall clock, and who has waited nineteen years. Answers by the first of the month.

volumes.title: The Solution, With Apologies
volumes.text:
Seven subscribers of The Locked Room Quarterly had it right, and so, before our last number was dry, did the culprit. Mr. Enoch Vesper walked up to Thistledown House on Sunday at one and set his cornet case on Mr. Thrupp's table. Inside, wrapped in a duster, was the Winter Queen.

He had palmed her as he closed her leather case, and carried her out before the bolt was shot. The room was never robbed while locked. The chime at three, built by him into the tall clock over many patient Sundays, was to prove her still there while he played on the bandstand.

Mr. Thrupp looked at the little device for a long time. Then he asked what a man owed for nineteen refusals. The Winter Queen now lives in Vesper's shop window, and visits Thistledown every Sunday at one. We apologise to the ghost.
